newsitem.title: SUDAN: US says Sudanese conflict "essentially domestic".
newsitem.headline: US says Sudanese conflict "essentially domestic".

text.p: The United States said on Thursday that the conflict in eastern Sudan was mainly domestic but the Sudanese government was trying to disguise this by reporting foreign intervention.
A statement by the U.S. embassy in Sudan also called for the release of politicians detained in Khartoum, apparently since a rebel offensive began in the east 11 days ago.

"Sudan's claims of foreign involvement in its civil war are an attempt to distract the Sudanese people and the international community from what is essentially a domestic political crisis," the statement said.
It went further on this point than State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns, who on Tuesday declined to comment on whether foreign countries were involved in the fighting.
The Sudanese government says Ethiopian and Eritrean forces are doing most of the fighting, but the rebels and the governments of the two neighbouring countries deny this.
The U.S. embassy statement gave no indication how many politicians the authorities has arrested.

But it said: "These actions do not address the Sudan government's political problems and raise human rights concerns. We urge the Sudanese government to respect fully the rights of all its citizens and call for the release of those detained."
The statement repeated Burns's call for a peaceful settlement through talks between the government and the rebels.
"We do not support a military overthrow of the government. We renew our call upon all parties to the civil war in Sudan to end this tragic conflict through peaceful negotiations.
"All elements of Sudanese society must participate in this dialogue of national reconciliation if Sudan is to embark on the road to peace and development," it said.

The embassy said $15 million in military aid to three of Sudan's neighbours -- Eritrea, Ethiopia and Uganda -- had not yet been delivered but that the U.S. government had authorised a further $4.75 million in 1997. "This assistance is intended to help those countries defend their territory from incursions by Sudanese-sponsored rebels," it added.
Opponents of the United States in the Middle East have cited the military aid as evidence that the Washington is behind the offensive by the rebel National Democratic Alliance.
